nameStory: The Thick-hooked Comb-tailed Spider gets its name from two key features that make it stand out in the spider world. Like all comb-tailed spiders, it has a row of bristles (called a calamistrum) on its hind legs that looks like a tiny comb, which it uses to spin special woolly silk. The 'thick-hooked' part refers to the robust, curved structures on the male's pedipalps - the small leg-like appendages near the mouth that male spiders use for mating.
description: The Thick-hooked Comb-tailed Spider is a small, brownish spider that most people would easily overlook in the leaf litter. These tiny hunters are only about 2-3 millimeters long - smaller than a pencil eraser - with relatively long legs for their body size. They belong to a family of spiders known for their unusual silk-spinning abilities, using their comb-like leg bristles to create woolly, tangled webs. With only one confirmed sighting in New England, this species is either extremely rare in our region or simply very good at staying hidden.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at just 2-3mm body length - about the size of a large grain of sand or small ant

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, somewhat flattened body with proportionally long, thin legs that feel delicate if gently touched

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally brownish coloration that blends seamlessly with dead leaves and soil - may appear almost dusty to the touch

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates small, irregular tangles of woolly silk that feel almost cotton-like compared to typical sticky spider webs

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves quickly through leaf litter and low vegetation, often running rather than jumping when disturbed

habitat: Look for Thick-hooked Comb-tailed Spiders in undisturbed forest floor environments with thick leaf litter, particularly in mixed hardwood or coniferous forests. They prefer areas with good moisture retention where small insects are abundant, often hiding under logs, rocks, or in the spaces between fallen leaves. Given the single New England record, they likely inhabit very specific microhabitats that we're still learning about.

seasonality.spring: Adults may become active as temperatures warm and prey insects emerge, though their small size makes spring detection challenging.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be found actively hunting and reproducing in the leaf litter.
seasonality.fall: May continue activity into early fall, with young spiders dispersing to new areas before winter arrives.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters in protected locations under deep leaf litter or logs, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Comb-tailed spiders like this species are essentially tiny textile artists - they use the comb-like bristles on their legs to card and fluff their silk into woolly threads, much like how people once combed sheep's wool into yarn, making them some of the most sophisticated silk-workers in the spider world.
confusionNotes: With only one New England record, confusion with other species is the main identification challenge. Any tiny brown spider in leaf litter could potentially be this species, but look for the characteristic woolly, tangled web rather than typical orb webs or funnel webs. Remember: if it's making cotton-candy-like silk, you might have found something special.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of records for this species in New England doesn't necessarily mean it's truly rare - it might simply reflect how difficult these tiny spiders are to find and identify. Many small ground-dwelling spiders are vastly under-recorded because they require specialized collecting techniques and expert identification to distinguish from similar species.
compareHints: Distinguishing this species from its relative Neoantistea agilis requires expert examination of microscopic features, particularly the male's reproductive structures that give this species its 'thick-hooked' name. Both species are tiny and brown, but magna tends to be slightly larger and more robust. In the field, any small comb-tailed spider in New England would need laboratory confirmation to determine which Neoantistea species you've found.
